title: what namaste actually says
hookLine: the word at the end of yoga class is how a lot of the world says hello

cards: Class ends. Everyone sits up, palms together, and the teacher says namaste. Then there's the mug that says namaste in bed.
In much of India and Nepal, it isn't a yoga word at all. It's how you greet your aunt, your neighbor, a guest at the door. And what it says is plainer, and kinder, than most people think.

teach.b: Namaste is Sanskrit, in two pieces. Namas, a bow. Te, to you.
People say it to elders, guests and strangers, usually with the palms pressed together at the chest and a small dip of the head. Sometimes the gesture says it with no word at all.

teach.h: THE LIGHT LINE IS A READING.
teach.b: You may have heard it means the light in me honors the light in you. That's a modern reading, not a translation.

It draws on a real idea some Hindu teachers find in the bow: that something sacred lives in every person, so you're bowing to that, not to someone's job or mood. So is it okay to say it in a yoga class?
Hindus don't all feel the same way about that, and it's worth knowing they differ. What tends to sting is the word as a punchline: on a beer can, or as a joke for leave me alone.
What tends to land is the plain thing it is: a greeting, meant. The difference isn't who's saying it. It's whether the bow is real.

how: In India and Nepal, people greet elders, guests and strangers with namaste or namaskar, palms pressed together at the chest and the head slightly bowed; many Hindus make the same gesture before images of the gods.

games.q: you're staying with a friend's family in India, and their grandmother comes to the door. which greeting fits best?
o: palms together, a small bow: namaste.
a wave from across the room.
games.why: a bow to you, with the hands: it's what the word is for, and many families greet an elder exactly this way.

games.q: build the word: a bow + to you.

practice: Three breaths with the bell. Bring your palms together at your chest, if you'd like. On the first breath, feel your hands meet.
On the second, bring to mind someone you'll see today. On the third, a small bow of the head, toward them, wherever they are.

wordCard.voice: Namaste. Namas, a bow; te, to you. A hello with respect inside it. Fourth word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: namas, a bow, plus te, to you. Namaskar is the same bow, as a noun.

carryVoice: Your line: mean the bow. Said that way, it's what it has always been in India and Nepal: a real greeting. Day four.
